implementation_notes: Hand-write the pair and publish with `sync/atomic`: `atomic.Pointer[Frame]` offers `Load`/`Store`/`Swap`/`CompareAndSwap`, and the package documents that all atomic operations behave as if executed in some sequentially consistent order - so one `Store` is a complete, portable swap and readers need no memory-order argument. `atomic.Value` does the same for interface values but panics if the concrete type changes, so use it only for a single value type. Readers must not mutate what they load; treat the published snapshot as frozen, or publish values instead of pointers.
pitfalls: Mutating the struct the published pointer points at re-creates the race; snapshots must be frozen after `Store`.
`atomic.Value` requires one concrete type per variable - storing a different type panics at runtime.
Copying a struct that embeds `atomic.Pointer`/`sync.Mutex` duplicates the synchronization state; `go vet` flags it (copylocks).

variants.name: RWMutex-guarded view (std-only, readable)
variants.idiom_name: sync.RWMutex + view() returning the current buffer
variants.implementation_notes: When readers must derive or copy from the buffer rather than just read a reference, `sync.RWMutex` with a `view()` method is more readable than lock-free tricks: the writer fills the back buffer and swaps under the write lock, readers take the read lock for the duration of their copy. It is the form to choose when the swap is rare; the cost is reader contention and the temptation to do real work while holding the lock. On the graphics side, `ebiten` owns the frame buffers and presents them, and `image/draw` supplies the compositing call, so no manual pair is needed there.
pitfalls: Doing heavy work (rendering, allocation, I/O) under `RLock` serializes the writer behind slow readers; copy out and release.
The swap must exchange both fields in one critical section - readers can see `current` and `next` individually, so a partial swap corrupts the pair.
`sync.RWMutex` is not reentrant and not copyable; embedding it by value in a struct that gets copied is a `go vet` error.
